newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canada dollar rallies on bank comments.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canada dollar rallies on bank comments.

text.p: Canada's dollar rose almost one U.S. cent on Thursday in its most volatile session since Quebec's 1995 sovereignty referendum, after Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen suggested the need for a shift to a less stimulative monetary policy.
The dollar rocketed to C$1.3710 (US$0.7293) in late trading after opening the North American session at C$1.3846 (US$0.7222). The currency closed on Wednesday at C$1.3893 (US$0.7197).
The rally prompted repeated intervention during the day by the Bank of Canada, which began selling Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars at the C$1.3828 (US$0.7231) level.
"The bank's been in everywhere. They're coming in every five or 10 points," one trader said.

The dollar began to rise after the central bank released its semi-annual monetary policy report, which indicated the bank's willingness to shift to a more neutral monetary policy from a stimulative one if inflation remained stable.

Strong fundamentals in the economy, low inflation and improvments in Canada's fiscal policy "continue to underpin market expectations of a future appreciation of the Canadian dollar," the report said.

Thiessen confirmed the bank's confidence in the currency when he told a news conference, "I really believe the underlying trend is upward and I know that on balance it has tended to be weak recently after the American interest rate move."
The prospect that the central bank would stop resisting future U.S. interest rate hikes had an immediate effect on the dollar as investors snapped up heavy volumes of Canadian bonds and securities.
Canadian bonds, which typically trade in the same direction as U.S. treasuries, were sharply higher today, while U.S. treasuries slumped.

"The idea that the bank is going to switch to a less stimulative monetary policy comes as a relief to the foreign exchange market," said Rob Palombi, senior fixed-income analyst for MMS International.
The Canadian dollar has depreciated by five percent since January, due mostly to concerns over diverging policies between the U.S. Federal Reserve and Canada's central bank.
"This rally is all about what is going right for the Canadian economy," Palombi said.
Analysts also said that early morning U.S. data indicating largely stable consumer prices helped prepare the Canada dollar for its impressive showing.
The U.S. Labor Department reported that the monthy Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.1 percent in April, as forecast last week by a Reuters survey of economists.
